---
title: "Bayesian modelling with brms"
subtitle: "Short workshop on demand · after Linear Models in R"
---






## What is brms?

[brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) is an R package for fitting **Bayesian regression models**, from simple linear models to complex multilevel models. You write the same formula syntax as in `lme4`, e.g. `y ~ x + (1 | id)`. brms translates the model into [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/), which estimates the posterior distribution of all parameters.

This makes brms an easy entry into Bayesian modelling for anyone who knows the models from *Linear Models in R*: the models stay the same, only the way of estimating them and of drawing conclusions changes.

## Topics

- Bayesian inference in a nutshell: prior, likelihood, posterior
- Choosing and checking priors (prior predictive checks)
- Fitting the course models in brms: linear models, GLMs, GLMMs
- Convergence diagnostics and posterior predictive checks
- Reporting: posterior summaries, credible intervals, predictions
- Link to [TAE](../tae/index.qmd): Bayes factors and the region of practical equivalence

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [Prior, posterior](../glossary.qmd#prior), [Credible interval](../glossary.qmd#credible-interval), [Rhat and effective sample size (ESS)](../glossary.qmd#rhat), [Divergent transitions](../glossary.qmd#divergent-transitions), [Convergence failure](../glossary.qmd#convergence)
:::

## Worked example: the Safe-vs-Risky box study

We return to the example from [session 11](../linear-models/sessions/11-glmm.qmd), with the same data. Chimpanzees choose into which of two boxes a grape is dropped. The **Safe** box clearly guarantees delivery; in the **Risky** box, the grape seems to get stuck. In fact, both boxes always deliver.

- **RQ1:** Do chimps prefer the Safe box in session 1?
- **RQ2:** Does this preference change over sessions?

::: {.box-warn}
The study (with the MPI EVA, Leipzig) is preregistered, but the data do not exist yet. As in session 11, the numbers are **made up to reflect what we expect**: 10 chimps × 4 sessions × 10 trials; response: choice (1 = Safe, 0 = Risky).
:::

### The data




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Data (same as session 11)"}
# Safe choices (out of 10) of 10 chimps in sessions 1-4
K <- rbind(c( 9, 10, 10, 10), c(10,  9,  9,  8), c(10, 10,  9,  7), c(10, 10,  6,  8),
           c( 5,  8,  8,  8), c( 8,  6,  6,  3), c( 5,  3,  2,  4), c( 5,  2,  3,  3),
           c( 1,  0,  1,  0), c( 1,  0,  0,  0))
cd <- data.frame(chimp = factor(rep(1:10, 4)), session = rep(1:4, each = 10), safe = c(K))

# trial-level data: one row per choice
set.seed(11)
trials <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cd)), function(i)
  data.frame(chimp = cd$chimp[i], session = cd$session[i],
             trial = (cd$session[i] - 1) * 10 + 1:10,
             choice = sample(rep(c(1, 0), c(cd$safe[i], 10 - cd$safe[i]))))))
trials$session_c <- trials$session - 1          # session 1 = 0
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
cd$p <- cd$safe / 10
avg  <- aggregate(p ~ session, data = cd, FUN = mean)

ggplot(cd, aes(session, p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_line(aes(group = chimp), colour = col_teal, alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(data = avg, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = avg, colour = col_red, size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "Safe choices",
       subtitle = "Thin lines: individual chimps · red: average")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/plot-data-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::




### Step 1: the GLMM from session 11




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
glmm <- glmer(choice ~ session_c + (1 + session_c | chimp),
              family = binomial, data = trials,
              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
```
:::

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


Table: Fixed effects (log-odds scale), Wald confidence intervals

|            | Estimate|   SE|         95% CI|     p|
|:-----------|--------:|----:|--------------:|-----:|
|(Intercept) |     0.91| 0.79|  [-0.63, 2.45]| 0.246|
|session_c   |    -0.36| 0.17| [-0.69, -0.03]| 0.030|


:::
:::




### Step 2: priors

A Bayesian model needs a prior for every parameter. We use **weakly informative priors** on the log-odds scale: they rule out absurd values but leave the data in charge.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),   # P(Safe) in session 1
            prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b"),           # change per session
            prior(exponential(0.5), class = "sd"),        # between-chimp SDs (mean 2)
            prior(lkj(2),         class = "cor"))         # intercept-slope correlation
```
:::




What do these priors imply *before* seeing any data? A **prior predictive check** translates them into chimp-level choice probabilities in session 1:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
set.seed(1)
p_session1 <- plogis(rnorm(1e4, 0, 1.5) + rnorm(1e4, 0, rexp(1e4, 0.5)))
ggplot(data.frame(p = p_session1), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = col_teal, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) in session 1 for a chimp, implied by the priors", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/prior-pred-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::




The priors allow chimps with strong Safe or strong Risky preferences, as in our data, where some chimps almost always and others almost never choose Safe.

### Step 3: fit the model

The formula is exactly the one from `glmer()`. `bernoulli` is the binomial family for single 0/1 choices.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- brm(choice ~ session_c + (1 + session_c | chimp),
           family = bernoulli, data = trials, prior = priors,
           chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 2026)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>   Links: mu = logit 
#> Formula: choice ~ session_c + (1 + session_c | chimp) 
#>    Data: trials (Number of observations: 400)

#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000

#> sd(session_c)                0.45      0.30     0.03     1.16 1.00     1008
#> cor(Intercept,session_c)    -0.01      0.40    -0.75     0.71 1.00     3411
#>                          Tail_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)                2042
#> sd(session_c)                1323
#> cor(Intercept,session_c)     2310
#> 
#> Population-Level Effects:

```


:::
:::




All `Rhat` values are close to 1.00 and the effective sample sizes (`ESS`) are large, so the four chains agree. The trace plots should look like "hairy caterpillars", with no chain drifting off:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(as.array(fit), pars = c("b_Intercept", "b_session_c", "sd_chimp__session_c"),
                      facet_args = list(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/trace-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::




### Step 4: answer the research questions with the posterior

The posterior is a distribution, so we can answer the research questions **on the response scale and as probabilities**.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
draws <- as_draws_df(fit)
p1 <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept)                            # session 1, average chimp
p4 <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept + 3 * draws$b_session_c)    # session 4, average chimp
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
post <- rbind(data.frame(session = "Session 1", p = p1), data.frame(session = "Session 4", p = p4))
ggplot(post, aes(p, fill = session)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_density(alpha = .6, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_teal, col_red), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) for an average chimp", y = "Posterior density")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/posterior-plot-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

:::




- **RQ1:** In session 1, an average chimp chooses the Safe box with probability 0.68, 95% credible interval [0.32, 0.92]. The posterior probability that the average chimp prefers Safe, i.e. that P(Safe) > .5, is 0.86. The interval is wide: with chimps that differ this much, 10 chimps say little about the average chimp's preference.
- **RQ2:** The change per session is -0.36 on the log-odds scale, 95% CrI [-0.83, 0.02]; the posterior probability of a decline is 0.97. From session 1 to session 4, P(Safe) changes by -0.23 for the average chimp, 95% CrI [-0.51, 0.01].

The model-implied curve for the average chimp, with 95% credible band:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
ce <- conditional_effects(fit, effects = "session_c")$session_c
ggplot(ce, aes(session_c + 1, estimate__)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower__, ymax = upper__), fill = col_teal, alpha = .25) +
  geom_line(colour = col_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "P(Safe)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/cond-effects-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::




### Step 5: does the model reproduce the data?

A **posterior predictive check** simulates new datasets from the fitted model and compares them with the observed data. Here: the proportion of Safe choices for each chimp.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
pp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", group = "chimp", ndraws = 1000) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1), labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of Safe choices") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/ppc-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::




The observed proportions (dark lines) lie well within the simulated ones for every chimp.

### Step 6: comparison with the GLMM from session 11




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
fe_b <- fixef(fit)
vc   <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(glmm))
sd_b <- summary(fit)$random$chimp

tab <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Intercept (session 1)", "Session", "SD intercept", "SD session slope", "Correlation"),
  glmer     = c(paste0(f2(cf[, 1]), " [", f2(ci[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[, 2]), "]"),
                f2(vc$sdcor[1]), f2(vc$sdcor[2]), f2(vc$sdcor[3])),
  brms      = paste0(f2(c(fe_b[, 1], sd_b[, 1])), " [",
                     f2(c(fe_b[, 3], sd_b[, 3])), ", ", f2(c(fe_b[, 4], sd_b[, 4])), "]"))
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrr",
             col.names = c("Parameter", "glmer: estimate [95% CI]", "brms: mean [95% CrI]"),
             caption = "Log-odds scale. glmer reports no intervals for the variance components by default.")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


Table: Log-odds scale. glmer reports no intervals for the variance components by default.

|Parameter             | glmer: estimate [95% CI]| brms: mean [95% CrI]|
|:---------------------|------------------------:|--------------------:|
|Intercept (session 1) |       0.91 [-0.63, 2.45]|   0.79 [-0.77, 2.42]|
|Session               |     -0.36 [-0.69, -0.03]|  -0.37 [-0.83, 0.02]|
|SD intercept          |                     2.32|    2.58 [1.54, 4.41]|
|SD session slope      |                     0.30|    0.45 [0.03, 1.16]|
|Correlation           |                    -0.26|  -0.01 [-0.75, 0.71]|


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
cmp <- data.frame(
  par   = rep(c("Intercept", "Session"), 2),
  model = rep(c("glmer (session 11)", "brms"), each = 2),
  est   = c(cf[, 1], fe_b[, 1]),
  lo    = c(ci[, 1], fe_b[, 3]),
  hi    = c(ci[, 2], fe_b[, 4]))
cmp$par <- factor(cmp$par, levels = c("Session", "Intercept"))

ggplot(cmp, aes(est, par, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = .5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_teal, col_red), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (log-odds) with 95% interval", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](bayesian-modelling_files/figure-html/compare-plot-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::




**What stays the same, and what changes**

- **The estimates agree, the intervals differ.** The posterior means are close to the `glmer()` estimates: Bayesian modelling is not a different model, but a different way of estimating it. The credible interval for the session effect is wider and just includes zero. The Wald interval of `glmer()` treats the estimated between-chimp SDs as known; the posterior also carries their uncertainty, which is large with only 10 chimps.
- **The interpretation changes.** A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability, given model and priors. That is how most people (mis)read a confidence interval anyway. And we can directly state things like "the probability that the preference declines over sessions is 0.97".
- **Uncertainty about the variance components is visible.** `glmer()` gives only point estimates for the between-chimp SDs and their correlation; brms gives full intervals. The wide intervals show how little 10 chimps tell us about individual differences.
- **Complex random-effects structures become easier.** With only 10 individuals, `glmer()` often runs into convergence warnings or singular fits. The priors keep brms stable, which helps with the maximal random-effects structures recommended for confirmatory tests.
- **The price:** more computing time (here a few minutes instead of a second) and the need to choose and justify priors.

## Prerequisites

*Linear Models in R*. Please install brms and a Stan backend ([rstan](https://mc-stan.org/rstan/) or [cmdstanr](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/)) before the workshop.
